claim: Shoot branching evolved independently in flowering plant sporophytes and moss gametophytes.
source: Shoot branching is a primary contributor to plant architecture, evolving independently in flowering plant sporophytes and moss gametophytes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but is presented as established knowledge.

claim: In Physcomitrella gametophytic shoots, lateral branches arise by re-specification of epidermal cells into branch initials.
source: We show that in gametophytic shoots of Physcomitrella, lateral branches arise by re-specification of epidermal cells into branch initials.
evidence: Supported by morphological and histological analysis shown in Figure 1, demonstrating branches differentiating from the epidermis.

claim: Three ancient hormonal regulators (auxin, cytokinin and strigolactone) interact to generate the branching pattern in Physcomitrella.
source: three known and ancient hormonal regulators of sporophytic branching interact to generate the branching pattern- auxin, cytokinin and strigolactone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data with hormone mutants and treatments shown in Figures 4-10.

claim: PIN-mediated basipetal auxin transport does not regulate branching patterns in Physcomitrella.
source: Although PIN-mediated basipetal auxin transport regulates branching patterns in flowering plants, this is not so in Physcomitrella, where bi-directional transport is required to generate realistic branching patterns.
evidence: Supported by model predictions (Figure 3) and experimental data with pin mutants and NPA treatments (Figure 8).

claim: Bi-directional auxin transport is required to generate realistic branching patterns in Physcomitrella.
source: Although PIN-mediated basipetal auxin transport regulates branching patterns in flowering plants, this is not so in Physcomitrella, where bi-directional transport is required to generate realistic branching patterns.
evidence: Supported by computational model simulations showing that KA/KB = 1 best approximates wild-type branching patterns (Figure 3, Table 1).

claim: Plasmodesmal connectivity is a potential mechanism for auxin transport in Physcomitrella branching.
source: Experiments with callose synthesis inhibitors suggest plasmodesmal connectivity as a potential mechanism for transport.
evidence: Supported by experiments with DDG (callose synthesis inhibitor) showing effects on branching patterns (Figure 9).

claim: The radiation of vascular plants was underpinned by the innovation of a branching growth habit around 430 million years ago.
source: The radiation of the vascular plants was underpinned by the innovation of a branching growth habit in the shoots of their last shared common ancestor around 430 million years ago (Langdale and Harrison, 2008; Edwards et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The earliest vascular plants branched by bifurcation.
source: The earliest vascular plants branched by bifurcation, involving the even partitioning of the growing tip into two new shoot tips (Sussex and Kerk, 2001; Harrison et al., 2005, 2007; Langdale and Harrison, 2008; Harrison and Langdale, 2010; Ligrone et al., 2012; Edwards et al., 2014; Tomescu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Lateral (axillary) branching evolved during diversification within seed plants.
source: Subsequent diversification within the seed plants was underpinned by the evolution of lateral (axillary) branching (Sussex and Kerk, 2001; Langdale and Harrison, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lateral branching permits finely tuned regulation of plant architecture in response to the environment.
source: Lateral branching thus permits finely tuned regulation of plant architecture and space filling in response to the environment (Bergamini and Peintinger, 2002; Domagalska and Leyser, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A capacity for lateral branching evolved by convergence in mosses and primed their diversification.
source: Whilst branching by bifurcation is prevalent in non-seed vascular plant sporophytes and many bryophyte gametophytes, a capacity for lateral branching evolved by convergence in mosses and primed their diversification (Farge-England, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In flowering plant sporophytes, axillary meristem initiation is regulated by a drop in auxin levels and a rise in cytokinin levels as leaves initiate from the apical meristem.
source: The mechanisms regulating lateral branching are well studied in flowering plant sporophytes, in which the initiation of axillary meristems is regulated by a drop in auxin levels and a rise in cytokinin levels as leaves initiate from the apical meristem (Wang et al., 2014a, 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The main shoot apex exerts an inhibitory effect over branch outgrowth, a phenomenon known as apical dominance.
source: Classical decapitation experiments showed that the main shoot apex exerts an inhibitory effect over subsequent branch outgrowth, a phenomenon known as apical dominance.
evidence: Supported by citations to classical experiments.

claim: Auxin can mediate the inhibition of branch outgrowth, and its action can be antagonized by cytokinin application to buds.
source: Replacing decapitated apices with lanolin impregnated with phytohormones showed that auxin can mediate this inhibition, and that its action can be antagonized by cytokinin application to buds (Thimann and Skoog, 1933; Wickson and Thimann, 1958; Cline, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Strigolactone exerts an inhibitory or stimulatory effect on branch outgrowth depending on the auxin transport status of the plant.
source: Strigolactone has recently been identified as a third hormonal regulator of branching, exerting an inhibitory or stimulatory effect on branch outgrowth depending on the auxin transport status of the plant (Gomez-Roldan et al., 2008; Umehara et al., 2008; Shinohara et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Regulated auxin transport plays a key role in the mechanism by which auxin, cytokinin and strigolactone regulate branching.
source: The mechanism by which the co-ordinated action of auxin, cytokinin and strigolactone regulates branching is not yet fully clear, but regulated auxin transport plays a key role (Crawford et al., 2010; Domagalska and Leyser, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Auxin is synthesized in young expanding leaves and is transported basipetally by PIN1 polar auxin efflux carriers to generate the polar auxin transport stream in the stem.
source: Auxin is synthesized in young expanding leaves and is transported basipetally by several transporters including PIN-FORMED1 (PIN1) polar auxin efflux carriers to generate the polar auxin transport stream in the stem (Gälweiler et al., 1998; Ljung et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The suppressive action of auxin on lateral branch outgrowth is mediated indirectly.
source: The suppressive action of auxin on lateral branch outgrowth is mediated indirectly (Morris, 1997; Booker et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Buds compete to export auxin into the main auxin transport stream and such competition is enhanced by a suppressive action of strigolactones on PIN1-mediated auxin transport.
source: However, a dominant bud need not be apical, and more recent work suggests that buds compete to export auxin into the main auxin transport stream and that such competition is enhanced by a suppressive action of strigolactones on PIN1-mediated auxin transport (Crawford et al., 2010; Prusinkiewicz et al., 2010; Shinohara et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PIN-mediated auxin transport is a key integration point in the regulation of branching patterns in flowering plants.
source: Thus, PIN-mediated auxin transport is a key integration point in the regulation of branching patterns.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding discussion of auxin transport mechanisms in flowering plants.

claim: Auxin (acting via polar transport) and cytokinin are conserved regulators of branching in vascular plant sporophytes.
source: Auxin transport assays and decapitation experiments used in conjunction with pharmacological treatments in the lycophyte, Selaginella, suggest that auxin (acting via polar transport) and cytokinin are conserved regulators of branching in vascular plant sporophytes (Williams, 1937; Wochok and Sussex, 1973, 1975; Sanders and Langdale, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is a detectable basipetal auxin transport stream in moss sporophytes.
source: Although bryophyte sporophytes do not normally branch, there is a detectable basipetal auxin transport stream in mosses (Fujita et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Physcomitrella, disruption of auxin transport can induce a branching form that resembles branching forms in the early fossil record.
source: In Physcomitrella, disruption of auxin transport by application of polar transport inhibitors or perturbations in PIN function can induce a branching form (Fujita et al., 2008; Bennett et al., 2014b) that closely resembles branching forms in the early fossil record
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bulk basipetal polar auxin transport is a conserved regulator of land plant sporophyte development.
source: These data suggest that bulk basipetal polar auxin transport is a conserved regulator of land plant sporophyte development, and point to a potential contribution of PIN-mediated polar auxin transport to the evolution of sporophytic branching (Fujita et al., 2008; Bennett et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on auxin transport in sporophytes.

claim: Classical decapitation experiments revealed apical dominance in mosses.
source: Classical decapitation experiments revealed apical dominance in mosses and showed that as in flowering plants, a suppressive role of the apex on lateral branching acts via auxin and can be antagonized by cytokinin (von Maltzahn, 1959).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In mosses, a suppressive role of the apex on lateral branching acts via auxin and can be antagonized by cytokinin.
source: Classical decapitation experiments revealed apical dominance in mosses and showed that as in flowering plants, a suppressive role of the apex on lateral branching acts via auxin and can be antagonized by cytokinin (von Maltzahn, 1959).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Physcomitrella PIN proteins are plasma-membrane targeted polar auxin transporters with many roles in gametophore development.
source: Whilst Physcomitrella PIN proteins are plasma-membrane targeted polar auxin transporters with many roles in gametophore development (Bennett et al., 2014a, 2014b; Viaene et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bulk basipetal auxin transport is not detected with radiolabelled auxin transport assays in moss gametophores.
source: bulk basipetal auxin transport is not detected with radiolabelled auxin transport assays in moss gametophores (Fujita et al., 2008; Fujita and Hasebe, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Strigolactone biosynthesis ppccd8 mutants have increased branching in protonemal tissues but no reported gametophore defects.
source: strigolactone biosynthesis ppccd8 mutants have increased branching in protonemal tissues but no reported gametophore defects (Proust et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Distinct developmental mechanisms have been recruited to regulate gametophyte and sporophyte shoot architecture in evolution.
source: These data have led to the hypothesis that distinct developmental mechanisms have been recruited to regulate gametophyte and sporophyte shoot architecture in evolution (Fujita et al., 2008; Fujita and Hasebe, 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature.

claim: Rhizoids initiate in all leaf axils beyond a certain distance from the main gametophore apex.
source: We found rhizoids initiating in all leaf axils beyond a certain distance from the main gametophore apex (Figure 1A–D)
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Branches are present in only a subset of axils in Physcomitrella.
source: but branches were present in only a subset of axils (Figure 1E–P).
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1E-P.

claim: There is no regular spacing in the pattern of initiation of Physcomitrella branches.
source: In contrast to reports from other species that have identified stereotypical and taxon-specific branch initiation patterns (Berthier et al., 1965; Berthier, 1970), we found no regular spacing in the pattern of initiation of Physcomitrella branches.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations and contrasts with cited literature on other species.

claim: There is no evidence of dormancy in Physcomitrella branches, suggesting that branch initiation and outgrowth are not distinct developmental processes.
source: We were unable to detect any evidence of dormancy, suggesting that branch initiation and outgrowth are not distinct developmental processes (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of observed dormancy in morphological analysis.

claim: At the earliest stage of branch initiation, branches appear as a single apical cell surrounded by leaf initials and adjacent to rhizoids.
source: At the earliest stage of branch initiation that we were able to detect, branches were manifest as a single apical cell surrounded by leaf initials and adjacent to rhizoids (Figure 1E–H)
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1E-H.

claim: Branches appear to differentiate from the epidermis in Physcomitrella.
source: appearing to differentiate from the epidermis (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by histological sections shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: Well developed lateral branches are morphologically similar to the main gametophore axis.
source: Well developed lateral branches were morphologically similar to the main gametophore axis (Figure 1M)
evidence: Supported by morphological observations shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Each branch persists as a superficial projection with no continuity between the conducting tissue of the lateral branches and the conducting tissue of the main stem.
source: transverse sections cut at the base of lateral branches showed that each branch persisted as a superficial projection; there was no continuity between the conducting tissue of the lateral branches and the conducting tissue of the main stem (Figure 1N–P).
evidence: Supported by histological sections shown in Figure 1N-P.

claim: Branch initiation in Physcomitrella is usually, but not invariably, acropetal.
source: These morphological data suggest that in Physcomitrella branches initiate de novo from the epidermis of the gametophore axis and that initiation is usually, but not invariably, acropetal.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of branch size relative to position shown in Figure 1Q.

claim: A minimum of 18 leaves is required prior to branch initiation in Physcomitrella.
source: The formation of a minimum of 18 leaves was required prior to branch initiation, and an apical portion devoid of branches was maintained at a similar length throughout development.
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in wild-type gametophores shown in Figure 2C.

claim: An apical portion devoid of branches (apical inhibition zone) is maintained at a similar length throughout development in Physcomitrella.
source: The formation of a minimum of 18 leaves was required prior to branch initiation, and an apical portion devoid of branches was maintained at a similar length throughout development.
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in wild-type gametophores shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In wild-type Physcomitrella, branches are more evenly dispersed than expected at random in the branching zone.
source: In the WT dataset, branches were more evenly dispersed than expected at random (p-value < 0.05; Figure 2D)
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of wild-type data to stochastic simulations.

claim: A stochastic model with imposed apical inhibition cannot produce a realistic branching pattern.
source: Even if an apical inhibition zone is introduced into a random model of branching, for example by assuming a branching competency that requires a minimum metamer age, it cannot produce a realistic branching pattern (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The main gametophore apex inhibits branching in Physcomitrella.
source: We first sought to identify potential contributions of the main gametophore apex and auxin to the branching pattern by performing surgical experiments in which thirty gametophores were teased out of several colonies and decapitated by removal of the top six metamers (the top third of the apical inhibition zone).
evidence: Supported by decapitation experiments shown in Figure 4, where removal of the apex led to branch initiation in the previously inhibited zone.

claim: Gametophores that had their apices replaced by lanolin discontinued growth of the main axis and initiated branches in the portion of the stem originally comprising the apical inhibition zone.
source: Whilst control gametophores continued to grow as normal (Figure 4B), the gametophores which had their apices replaced by lanolin discontinued growth of the main axis and initiated branches in the portion of the stem originally comprising the apical inhibition zone beneath the cut site (Figure 4C,E).
evidence: Supported by decapitation experiments shown in Figure 4C,E.

claim: Gametophores that had their apices replaced by IAA impregnated lanolin had impaired branch initiation and development.
source: In contrast, the gametophores that had their apices replaced by IAA impregnated lanolin had impaired branch initiation and development (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Supported by decapitation experiments with IAA treatment shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: Mean IAA levels are highest in the tip of Physcomitrella gametophores.
source: We therefore quantified IAA levels along the gametophore axis by sampling the top six metamers, the apical inhibition zone minus the tip and the branching zone with the branches removed (Figure 4A). Despite some variability between replicates, we found that mean IAA levels were highest in the tip.
evidence: Supported by IAA quantification data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: GH3::GUS signal intensity drops substantially in decapitated Physcomitrella plants.
source: We also undertook decapitation experiments in the GH3::GUS reporter line and found that the signal intensity dropped substantially in decapitated plants
evidence: Supported by GH3::GUS reporter analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The apex can affect auxin levels elsewhere in the Physcomitrella gametophore.
source: We also undertook decapitation experiments in the GH3::GUS reporter line and found that the signal intensity dropped substantially in decapitated plants, consistent with the notion that the apex can affect auxin levels elsewhere in the gametophore.
evidence: This is inferred from the GH3::GUS reporter data after decapitation.

claim: Auxin treatment increases the size of the apical inhibition zone in Physcomitrella.
source: For all the treatments, the size of the apical inhibition zone significantly increased, the branch number was strongly reduced and branch initiation in the branching zone significantly decreased, suggesting that auxin can act as a global suppressor of branching.
evidence: Supported by auxin treatment experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Auxin treatment reduces branch number in Physcomitrella.
source: For all the treatments, the size of the apical inhibition zone significantly increased, the branch number was strongly reduced and branch initiation in the branching zone significantly decreased
evidence: Supported by auxin treatment experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Auxin can act as a global suppressor of branching in Physcomitrella.
source: For all the treatments, the size of the apical inhibition zone significantly increased, the branch number was strongly reduced and branch initiation in the branching zone significantly decreased, suggesting that auxin can act as a global suppressor of branching.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of auxin treatments on branching patterns shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Ppshi2-1 mutant has reduced auxin synthesis at the gametophore apex.
source: The branching phenotype of Ppshi2-1, an auxin-deficient mutant in which auxin synthesis at the gametophore apex is reduced (Eklund et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Ppshi2-1 mutant has a reduced apical inhibition zone and increased branch density within the branching zone.
source: The branching phenotype of Ppshi2-1, an auxin-deficient mutant in which auxin synthesis at the gametophore apex is reduced (Eklund et al., 2010), matched this predicted outcome (Figure 6C,E,G,I,J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Video 7).
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in shi2-1 mutants shown in Figure 6.

claim: PpSHI ox-5 is a transgenic line with elevated auxin levels.
source: The branching pattern of PpSHI ox-5, a transgenic line with elevated auxin levels (Eklund et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The PpSHI ox-5 transgenic line has an increased apical inhibition zone and decreased branch density.
source: The branching pattern of PpSHI ox-5, a transgenic line with elevated auxin levels (Eklund et al., 2010), again matched the model output (Figure 6D,F,H,I,J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Video 8).
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in SHI ox-5 transgenics shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cytokinin antagonizes the suppressive effects of auxin in promoting branching in flowering plants and moss.
source: In bud treatment experiments in flowering plants and moss, cytokinin antagonizes the suppressive effects of auxin in promoting branching (Thimann and Skoog, 1933; Wickson and Thimann, 1958; von Maltzahn, 1959)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CKX2oe transgenics have reduced cytokinin levels.
source: The branching pattern of a transgenic line that constitutively expresses the Arabidopsis cytokinin degradation gene, CYTOKININ OXIDASE-2 (CKX2oe) (von Schwartzenberg et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CKX2oe transgenics have fewer branches and a larger apical inhibition zone.
source: The branching pattern of a transgenic line that constitutively expresses the Arabidopsis cytokinin degradation gene, CYTOKININ OXIDASE-2 (CKX2oe) (von Schwartzenberg et al., 2007), was quantified and found to be similar to the model output in having fewer branches and a larger apical inhibition zone (Figure 7C,E,G,I,J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Video 9).
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in CKX2oe transgenics shown in Figure 7.

claim: IPT1oe transgenics have upregulated cytokinin levels.
source: To test this hypothesis, we generated Physcomitrella ISOPENTENYL TRANSFERASE-1 (von Schwartzenberg et al., 2007) transgenics (IPT1oe) in which cytokinin levels are upregulated (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by cytokinin profiling data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: IPT1oe transgenics have a reduced apical inhibition zone and increased branch number.
source: the branching pattern in the IPT1oe line was similar (Figure 7D,F,H,I,J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in IPT1oe transgenics shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cytokinin application promotes meristematic cell formation and proliferation along the gametophore axis.
source: Moreover, cytokinin application to gametophores was sufficient to promote meristematic cell formation and proliferation along the gametophore axis (Figure 7K–N).
evidence: Supported by cytokinin treatment experiments shown in Figure 7K-N.

claim: Cytokinin is necessary for and promotes branching and lateral meristem activity in Physcomitrella.
source: Thus cytokinin is necessary for and promotes branching and lateral meristem activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on cytokinin mutants and treatments.

claim: PIN-mediated auxin transport is not a major contributor to branching patterns in Physcomitrella.
source: Thus PIN-mediated auxin transport is not a major contributor to branching patterns.
evidence: Supported by analysis of pin mutants and NPA treatments shown in Figure 8.

claim: ABCB/PGP proteins do not regulate branching in Physcomitrella.
source: We found no difference between mock and BUM-treated plants suggesting that ABCB/PGP proteins do not regulate branching in Physcomitrella.
evidence: Supported by BUM treatment experiments shown in Figure 8X-AB.

claim: Callose-gated plasmodesmal connectivity is a plausible mechanism to regulate branching patterns in Physcomitrella.
source: These data suggest callose-gated plasmodesmal connectivity as a plausible mechanism to regulate branching patterns in Physcomitrella.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of DDG (callose synthesis inhibitor) on branching patterns shown in Figure 9.

claim: The strigolactone biosynthesis gene ppccd8 is expressed at the base of gametophores.
source: We noted from published literature (Proust et al., 2011) that the strigolactone biosynthesis gene ppccd8 is expressed at the base of gametophores.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: ppccd8 mutants have strongly increased branch activation at the base of gametophores.
source: We found strongly increased branch activation at the base of gametophores (number of branching gametophores: WT, 4/60; ppccd8 mutant, 29/60) (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in ppccd8 mutants shown in Figure 10.

claim: GR24 is able to suppress basal branch formation in ppccd8 mutants.
source: To confirm that the ppccd8 mutant phenotype was caused by a deficiency in strigolactone production, we quantified the branching pattern in ppccd8 mutants grown on medium supplemented with 1 μM GR24, a synthetic strigolactone analogue, and found that GR24 was able to suppress basal branch formation (Figure 10C).
evidence: Supported by GR24 treatment experiments shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Branching is very strongly suppressed in RMS1 overexpressing transgenics.
source: To evaluate whether strigolactone can act as a global branch suppressor, we analysed the branching pattern in Physcomitrella mutants that over express the pea strigolactone synthesis gene, RMS1 (Proust et al., 2011). We found that branching was very strongly suppressed in this transgenic line (Figure 10D, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis of branching patterns in RMS1oe transgenics shown in Figure 10.

claim: Basal expression of a strigolactone biosynthetic gene can account for the predicted requirement for a local basal inhibitor of branching.
source: Thus basal expression of a strigolactone biosynthetic gene can account for the predicted requirement of our model for a local basal inhibitor of branching.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on ppccd8 expression, mutant phenotypes, and model predictions.

claim: Hormonal signalling by auxin, cytokinin and strigolactone evolved before plants' transition to land.
source: Hormonal signalling by auxin, cytokinin and strigolactone evolved before plants' transition to land (Cooke et al., 2002; De Smet et al., 2011; Delaux et al., 2013; Gruhn and Heyl, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Auxin and cytokinin were recruited to regulate axillary bud initiation in flowering plant sporophytes.
source: and was recruited to regulate axillary bud initiation (auxin and cytokinin; [Wang et al., 2014a, 2014b])
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Auxin, cytokinin and strigolactone regulate lateral branch outgrowth in flowering plant sporophytes.
source: and lateral branch outgrowth in flowering plant sporophytes (Domagalska and Leyser, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The ratio c/T determines the fate of epidermal cells in the Physcomitrella gametophore axis.
source: In combination our model and experimental data lead us to a notion of branching whereby the ratio c/T determines the fate of epidermal cells in the gametophore axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined model and experimental results.

claim: If the ratio c/T drops below a threshold level, an epidermal cell can be respecified as a lateral apical cell thereby triggering branch initiation.
source: If the ratio drops below a threshold level, an epidermal cell can be respecified as a lateral apical cell thereby triggering branch initiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the model assumptions and experimental validation.

claim: Cells elsewhere in the metamer are competent to form branch initials if the c/T ratio is perturbed.
source: However, cells elsewhere in the metamer are also competent to form branch initials, and do so if the c/T ratio is perturbed, for instance by changing auxin (Figures 5, 6), strigolactone (Figure 9) or cytokinin levels (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ectopic branch formation with hormone treatments.

claim: Key strigolactone signalling components required for the inhibition of sporophyte branching in higher plants are not present in mosses.
source: Notably, key strigolactone signalling components required for the inhibition of sporophyte branching in higher plants are not present in mosses (Delaux et al., 2013; de Saint Germain et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: D14 and D53 are absent in Physcomitrella.
source: For instance, components such as D14 (involved in strigolactone perception) and D53 are absent in Physcomitrella (Challis et al., 2013; Delaux et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Physcomitrella homologue of MAX2 may not be involved in strigolactone signalling.
source: Similarly the Physcomitrella homologue of the F-Box protein MAX2 may not be involved in strigolactone signalling, despite its central role in many strigolactone responses in flowering plants (de Saint Germain et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The ancestral function of strigolactone and/or strigolactone-like signals is thought to be in rhizoid elongation.
source: Although there is a substantial body of evidence that strigolactone-like signals are active across the plant kingdom, the ancestral function of strigolactone and/or these strigolactone-like signals is thought to be in rhizoid elongation (Delaux et al., 2013; de Saint Germain et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The absence of distinct branch initiation and outgrowth processes in Physcomitrella implicates strigolactone in branch initiation.
source: The absence of distinct branch initiation and outgrowth processes in Physcomitrella implicates strigolactone in branch initiation
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that branch initiation and outgrowth are not distinct processes and the effects of strigolactone on branching.

claim: Gametophytic branching forms have several independent evolutionary origins.
source: Although plant phylogenies show that gametophytic branching forms have several independent evolutionary origins, the innovation of sporophytic branching maps once onto the plant tree of life (Langdale and Harrison, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The innovation of sporophytic branching maps once onto the plant tree of life.
source: Although plant phylogenies show that gametophytic branching forms have several independent evolutionary origins, the innovation of sporophytic branching maps once onto the plant tree of life (Langdale and Harrison, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sporophytic branching occurred in pre-vascular plants such as Partitatheca.
source: and occurred in pre-vascular plants such as Partitatheca (Edwards et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The antagonistic relationship between auxin and cytokinin in the regulation of branching is conserved within the vascular plants.
source: Exogenous hormone treatments in Selaginella have shown that the antagonistic relationship between auxin and cytokinin in the regulation of branching is conserved within the vascular plants (Sanders and Langdale, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Auxin transport-mediated apical dominance is a homology of vascular plant sporophytes.
source: Furthermore, auxin transport assays and pharmacological treatments used in combination with decapitation in Selaginella (Williams, 1937; Wochok and Sussex, 1973, 1975) have shown that auxin transport-mediated apical dominance is a homology of vascular plant sporophytes.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Auxin transport-regulated branching may be a homology of the sporophyte generation.
source: Disruption of PIN-mediated polar auxin transport in moss sporophytes can induce a branching form that is intermediate between living bryophytes and vascular plants (Fujita et al., 2008; Bennett et al., 2014b), and resembles the earliest branching forms in the sporophytic fossil record (Edwards et al., 2014), suggesting that auxin transport-regulated branching may be a homology of the sporophyte generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature on auxin transport effects in moss sporophytes.

claim: The mode and basis of auxin transport are a key divergence point in branch patterning mechanisms between land plant sporophytes and gametophytes.
source: Although the regulation of lateral branching by three key regulatory hormone pathways in moss gametophytes indicates deep homology (Scotland, 2010), the mode and basis of auxin transport are a key divergence point in branch patterning mechanisms between land plant sporophytes and gametophytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental and modeling results showing different auxin transport mechanisms.
